claim: The atypical cadherins Fat and Dachsous (Ds) signal through the Hippo pathway to regulate growth of numerous organs, including the Drosophila wing.
source: The atypical cadherins Fat and Dachsous (Ds) signal through the Hippo pathway to regulate growth of numerous organs, including the Drosophila wing.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Fat-Ds signaling and the Hippo pathway in organ growth regulation.

claim: Ds-Fat signaling tunes a unique feature of cell proliferation found to control the rate of wing growth during the third instar larval phase.
source: Here, we find that Ds-Fat signaling tunes a unique feature of cell proliferation found to control the rate of wing growth during the third instar larval phase.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The duration of the cell cycle increases in direct proportion to the size of the wing during the third instar.
source: The duration of the cell cycle increases in direct proportion to the size of the wing, leading to linear-like growth during the third instar.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: Cell cycle duration increasing in direct proportion to wing size leads to linear-like growth during the third instar.
source: The duration of the cell cycle increases in direct proportion to the size of the wing, leading to linear-like growth during the third instar.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed relationship between cell cycle duration and wing size.

claim: Ds-Fat signaling enhances the rate at which the cell cycle lengthens with wing size.
source: Ds-Fat signaling enhances the rate at which the cell cycle lengthens with wing size, thus diminishing the rate of wing growth.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 showing different scaling coefficients in control versus RNAi knockdown conditions.

claim: Ds-Fat signaling diminishes the rate of wing growth by enhancing the rate at which the cell cycle lengthens with wing size.
source: Ds-Fat signaling enhances the rate at which the cell cycle lengthens with wing size, thus diminishing the rate of wing growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed effects of Ds-Fat signaling on cell cycle dynamics and wing growth rates.

claim: Ds-Fat signaling results in a complex but stereotyped relative scaling of wing growth with body growth in Drosophila.
source: We show that this results in a complex but stereotyped relative scaling of wing growth with body growth in Drosophila.
evidence: This is supported by allometric growth data shown in Figures 1G and 4E.

claim: Fat and Ds protein distributions in the wing are graded and change during growth.
source: Finally, we examine the dynamics of Fat and Ds protein distribution in the wing, observing graded distributions that change during growth.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: The significance of Fat and Ds protein gradient dynamics is unclear since perturbations in expression have negligible impact on wing growth.
source: However, the significance of these dynamics is unclear since perturbations in expression have negligible impact on wing growth.
evidence: This is based on experimental manipulations of Fat and Ds gradients shown in Figure 7.

claim: The rate of growth over time is internally regulated with an upper limit set independent of environmental factors such as nutrition.
source: The rate of growth over time is internally regulated with an upper limit set independent of such environmental factors as nutrition (Conlon and Raff, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The size setpoint when growth ceases is internally controlled.
source: The size setpoint when growth ceases is also internally controlled (Leevers and McNeill, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The size setpoint is typically reached when the animal transitions to adulthood.
source: Typically, the setpoint is reached when the animal transitions to adulthood.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established biological knowledge.

claim: Growth rate control and growth arrest control processes are linked with one another.
source: The two control processes are linked with one another.
evidence: This is supported by the example of insulin signaling mutants cited in the text.

claim: Drosophila that are deficient in insulin signaling grow slowly and their final size setpoint is smaller than normal.
source: For example, Drosophila that are deficient in insulin signaling grow slowly and their final size setpoint is smaller than normal (Rulifson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Sometimes the growth-arrest process compensates for an abnormal growth rate to generate a normal size setpoint.
source: However, sometimes the growth-arrest process compensates for an abnormal growth rate to generate a normal size setpoint (Leevers and McNeill, 2005; Penzo-Méndez and Stanger, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The wing of Drosophila is a well-established model system to study organ growth control.
source: The wing of Drosophila is a well-established model system to study organ growth control.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: In Drosophila larvae, the anlage fated to form the adult wing blade is composed of an epithelial domain embedded within a larger epithelial sheet named the wing imaginal disc or wing disc.
source: In Drosophila larvae, the anlage fated to form the adult wing blade is composed of an epithelial domain embedded within a larger epithelial sheet named the wing imaginal disc or wing disc (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The wing pouch anlage is surrounded by wing disc cells that will form the wing hinge and notum, which is the dorsal thorax.
source: The anlage, called the wing pouch, is surrounded by wing disc cells that will form the wing hinge and notum, which is the dorsal thorax.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Two wing discs reside within the body cavity of a larva.
source: Two wing discs reside within the body cavity of a larva (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Wing discs continuously grow as the larva grows and undergoes three successive molts, from first to second to third instar.
source: They continuously grow as the larva grows and undergoes three successive molts, from first to second to third instar.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Wing discs grow exponentially by asynchronous cell division until the mid-third larval stage.
source: Wing discs grow exponentially by asynchronous cell division until the mid-third larval stage, when growth becomes linear-like, and finally stops when the late third instar larva undergoes its transition to the pupal stage (Fain and Stevens, 1982; Graves and Schubiger, 1982; Bryant and Levinson, 1985; Neto-Silva et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Wing disc growth becomes linear-like at the mid-third larval stage.
source: Wing discs grow exponentially by asynchronous cell division until the mid-third larval stage, when growth becomes linear-like, and finally stops when the late third instar larva undergoes its transition to the pupal stage (Fain and Stevens, 1982; Graves and Schubiger, 1982; Bryant and Levinson, 1985; Neto-Silva et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Wing disc growth stops when the late third instar larva undergoes its transition to the pupal stage.
source: Wing discs grow exponentially by asynchronous cell division until the mid-third larval stage, when growth becomes linear-like, and finally stops when the late third instar larva undergoes its transition to the pupal stage (Fain and Stevens, 1982; Graves and Schubiger, 1982; Bryant and Levinson, 1985; Neto-Silva et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and confirmed by data in Figure 1E.

claim: During pupation, each wing pouch develops into a single adult wing blade.
source: During pupation, each wing pouch develops into a single adult wing blade.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Larval body weight increased linearly from 3.0 to 4.0 days after egg laying (AEL).
source: Larval body weight increased linearly from 3.0 to 4.0 days AEL, followed by a 12 hr period of slower growth, and thereafter weight remained constant (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: After 4.0 days AEL, larval body weight showed a 12 hr period of slower growth, and thereafter weight remained constant.
source: Larval body weight increased linearly from 3.0 to 4.0 days AEL, followed by a 12 hr period of slower growth, and thereafter weight remained constant (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The time point at which larvae stopped growing (4.5 days AEL) coincided with the time at which they stopped feeding and underwent a 12 hr non-feeding stage.
source: The time point at which larvae stopped growing (4.5 days AEL) coincided with the time at which they stopped feeding and underwent a 12 hr non-feeding stage (Slaidina et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1B and a citation to previous work on larval feeding behavior.

claim: Weight remained constant during the one-hr-long white pre-pupal (WPP) stage and also one hr later (WPP + 1 stage).
source: Weight remained constant during the one-hr-long white pre-pupal (WPP) stage and also one hr later (WPP + 1 stage; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Wing pouch volume appeared to increase linearly over time during the early-to-late third instar stage.
source: Wing pouch volume appeared to increase linearly over time and continued to grow during the non-feeding larval stage (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Wing pouch volume continued to grow during the non-feeding larval stage.
source: Wing pouch volume appeared to increase linearly over time and continued to grow during the non-feeding larval stage (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Growth of the wing pouch ceased at the WPP stage.
source: Growth of the wing pouch ceased at the WPP stage (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At the third instar larval stage, dividing cells were observed throughout the wing pouch.
source: At the third instar larval stage, dividing cells were observed throughout the wing pouch (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and B)
evidence: This is supported by PHH3 staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: At the WPP stage, dividing cells were only found in a narrow zone where sensory organ precursor cells undergo two divisions to generate future sensory organs.
source: whereas at the WPP stage, dividing cells were only found in a narrow zone where sensory organ precursor cells undergo two divisions to generate future sensory organs (Nolo et al., 2000 Figure 1—figure supplement 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by PHH3 staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C and D, and a citation to previous work.

claim: The hinge/notum domain of the wing disc showed similar linear-like growth trajectory as the wing pouch during the early-to-late third instar.
source: A similar linear-like growth trajectory was observed for the notum-hinge as for the wing pouch, although the hinge/notum stopped growing during the non-feeding stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and B.

claim: The hinge/notum stopped growing during the non-feeding stage.
source: A similar linear-like growth trajectory was observed for the notum-hinge as for the wing pouch, although the hinge/notum stopped growing during the non-feeding stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and B.

claim: Volumetric measurements are consistent with earlier studies that found wing disc growth is linear-like, as measured by cell number, during the mid-to-late third instar.
source: Overall, our volumetric measurements are consistent with earlier studies that found wing disc growth is linear-like, as measured by cell number, during the mid-to-late third instar (Fain and Stevens, 1982; Graves and Schubiger, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of current data with citations to previous work.

claim: For most animal species, allometric growth of organs follows a power law.
source: For most animal species, allometric growth of organs follows a power law (Huxley and Teissier, 1936), such that logarithmic transformation of the organ and body size measurements fits a linear relationship (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and illustrated in Figure 1F.

claim: When the organ grows at the same rate as the body, it exhibits isometric growth.
source: When the organ grows at the same rate as the body, it exhibits isometric growth (Huxley and Teissier, 1936).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: When the organ grows at a faster or slower rate than the body, it has positive or negative allometric growth, respectively.
source: When the organ grows at a faster or slower rate than the body, it has positive or negative allometric growth, respectively (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a definition illustrated in Figure 1F.

claim: In the silkworm, its wing disc grows linearly with its body while the larva feeds, but then continues its linear growth after larvae have ceased feeding.
source: For example, in the silkworm, its wing disc grows linearly with its body while the larva feeds, but then continues its linear growth after larvae have ceased feeding (Williams, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Silkworm wing disc allometric growth has two phases: the first is isometric and the second is positively allometric.
source: Thus, its allometric growth has two phases: the first is isometric and the second is positively allometric.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited silkworm wing disc growth pattern.

claim: Allometric growth of the Drosophila wing pouch had two phases, both of which showed positive allometry.
source: As with silkworms, allometric growth of the wing pouch had two phases, both of which showed positive allometry.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The inflection point in wing pouch allometric growth was the time when larvae ceased feeding.
source: The inflection point was the time when larvae ceased feeding.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Allometric growth of the notum-hinge exhibited two phases, although growth in the second phase was more limited than that observed for the wing pouch.
source: Allometric growth of the notum-hinge also exhibited two phases, although growth in the second phase was more limited than that observed for the wing pouch (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5C.

claim: Allometric growth control of the wing imaginal disc appears to be composed of multiple mechanisms.
source: Therefore, allometric growth control of the wing imaginal disc appears to be composed of multiple mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed two-phase allometric growth patterns.

claim: Cells transcribe the ds gene at different levels depending upon their position in the wing disc.
source: Qualitative measurements of ds gene expression found that cells transcribe the gene at different levels depending upon their position in the wing disc (Strutt and Strutt, 2002; Ma et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and confirmed by smFISH data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is graded transcription of ds across the wing pouch.
source: We confirmed that there is graded transcription across the pouch by using single molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization (smFISH) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A model hypothesized that the ds transcriptional gradient generates a Ds protein gradient across the wing pouch, and the gradient regulates growth by inducing Fat signaling in cells.
source: A model hypothesized that this transcriptional gradient generates a Ds protein gradient across the wing pouch, and the gradient regulates growth by inducing Fat signaling in cells (Pan, 2010).
evidence: This is a model from previous work cited in the text.

claim: According to the gradient model, if the Ds gradient becomes flattened, it leads to growth cessation.
source: If the Ds gradient becomes flattened, it leads to growth cessation.
evidence: This is a prediction from the cited model.

claim: There was a graded distribution of Ds-GFP along both anterior-posterior (AP) and dorsal-ventral (DV) axes of the wing pouch.
source: There was a graded distribution of Ds-GFP along both anterior-posterior (AP) and dorsal-ventral (DV) axes of the wing pouch.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Ds was high near the pouch border and low at the center of the pouch.
source: Ds was high near the pouch border and low at the center of the pouch (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The Ds gradient was asymmetric along the AP axis, being lower along the anterior pouch border than posterior border.
source: The gradient was asymmetric along the AP axis, being lower along the anterior pouch border than posterior border.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: As the pouch grew larger, the Ds gradient appeared to become progressively shallower.
source: As the pouch grew larger, the Ds gradient appeared to become progressively shallower.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: When normalized to pouch size, the Ds-GFP profiles along the AP axis collapsed together.
source: When we normalized all of the Ds-GFP profiles to their corresponding pouch sizes, the profiles along the AP axis collapsed together (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by normalized fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Along the DV axis, the normalized Ds-GFP profiles remained distinct because both maximum and minimum limits of Ds-GFP progressively diminished as the wing pouch grew.
source: In contrast, along the DV axis the normalized profiles remained distinct because both maximum and minimum limits of Ds-GFP progressively diminished as the wing pouch grew (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by normalized fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Fat-GFP had a graded distribution along both the AP and DV axes of the wing pouch; low near the pouch border and high at the center of the wing pouch.
source: Surprisingly, Fat-GFP had a graded distribution along both the AP and DV axes of the wing pouch; low near the pouch border and high at the center of the wing pouch (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: The Fat gradient profile was opposite to the one observed for Ds-GFP.
source: The gradient profile was opposite to the one we observed for Ds-GFP.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of Fat-GFP and Ds-GFP gradient data.

claim: As the pouch grew in size, the Fat gradient appeared to grow shallower, and it became flat along the AP axis at the WPP stage.
source: As the pouch grew in size, the Fat gradient appeared to grow shallower, and it became flat along the AP axis at the WPP stage.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2G.

claim: When normalized to pouch size, the Fat-GFP profiles did not collapse.
source: When we normalized all the Fat-GFP profiles to their corresponding pouch sizes, the profiles did not collapse (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: This is supported by normalized fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2I and J.

claim: The minimum limit of Fat-GFP was conserved but the maximum limit of Fat-GFP progressively diminished as the wing pouch grew.
source: The minimum limit of Fat-GFP was conserved but the maximum limit of Fat-GFP progressively diminished as the wing pouch grew.
evidence: This is supported by normalized fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2I and J.

claim: The graded distribution of Fat protein was surprising since it was reported that fat gene transcription is uniform.
source: The graded distribution of Fat protein was surprising since it was reported that fat gene transcription is uniform (Garoia et al., 2000), which we confirmed by smFISH (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and a citation to previous work.

claim: Fat protein expressed under UAS-da-Gal4 control was graded in a similar pattern to endogenous Fat.
source: However, Fat protein was graded in a similar pattern to endogenous Fat (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2L.

claim: The Fat gradient is generated by a post-transcriptional mechanism.
source: Thus, the Fat gradient is generated by a post-transcriptional mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that uniform transcription produces a graded protein distribution.

claim: The distribution of Fat was unchanged in a fj mutant.
source: However, the distribution of Fat was unchanged in a fj mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Ds levels were unchanged in the fj mutant.
source: Additionally, Ds levels were unchanged in the fj mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D)
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: There was no difference in wing pouch volume in fj mutants compared to wildtype.
source: and there was no difference in wing pouch volume in fj mutants compared to wildtype (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is supported by volume measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E.

claim: In a ds mutant, the level of Fat-GFP at the wing pouch center was identical to wildtype but the level of Fat-GFP near the pouch border was abnormally high.
source: The level of Fat-GFP at the wing pouch center was identical to wildtype but the level of Fat-GFP near the pouch border was abnormally high (Figure 2M).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2M.

claim: In a ds mutant, the flattened Fat-GFP profile was not observed at the WPP stage.
source: Furthermore, we did not observe the flattened Fat-GFP profile at the WPP stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: In a ds mutant, the Fat-GFP profile remained weakly graded at the WPP stage and was flattened somewhat more by the WPP + 1 stage.
source: Instead, the Fat-GFP profile remained weakly graded at the WPP stage and was flattened somewhat more by the WPP + 1 stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Ma et al., 2003 observed upregulation of Fat along cell junctions between ds mutant cells of the pupal wing.
source: However, Ma et al., 2003 observed upregulation of Fat along cell junctions between ds mutant cells of the pupal wing, which is consistent with our observations of Fat-GFP upregulation near the pouch border of a ds mutant disc (Figure 2M).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and comparison with current data.

claim: The Ds gradient scales with the size of the wing pouch as measured along the length of the AP axis of symmetry.
source: The Ds gradient scales with the size of the wing pouch as measured along the length of the AP axis of symmetry (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by normalized fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Knockdown of perlecan expression by RNAi causes wing disc cells to become thinner and more elongated due to the altered extracellular matrix in the wing disc.
source: Knockdown of perlecan expression by RNAi causes wing disc cells to become thinner and more elongated due to the altered extracellular matrix in the wing disc (Kirkland et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: actin5C>trol(RNAi) caused a reduction in the area of the wing pouch and an increase in the thickness of the wing pouch at the WPP stage.
source: We measured the dimensions of the wing pouch at the WPP stage and observed that actin5C>trol(RNAi) caused a reduction in the area of the wing pouch and an increase in the thickness of the wing pouch (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The overall change in pouch dimensions from actin5C>trol(RNAi) had no effect on wing pouch volume.
source: The overall change in pouch dimensions had no effect on wing pouch volume (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by volume measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: actin5C>trol(RNAi) had no effect on the Ds-GFP gradient at WPP stage.
source: We then measured the Ds-GFP profile at WPP stage and found actin5C>trol(RNAi) had no effect on the gradient (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Ds appears to scale with the volume and not the area of the wing pouch.
source: Thus, Ds appears to scale with the volume and not the area of the wing pouch.
evidence: This is an inference based on the trol(RNAi) experiment results.

claim: The Fat gradient flattened normally at the WPP stage in actin5C>trol(RNAi) animals.
source: We also examined Fat-GFP to see if its dynamics were altered, and found the gradient flattened normally at the WPP stage (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: en>RBF overexpression resulted in half the number of cells in the P compartment but they were twofold larger in size, such that the P compartment size was unchanged relative to the anterior (A) compartment.
source: Previous work had found such overexpression resulted in half the number of cells in the P compartment but they were twofold larger in size, such that the P compartment size was unchanged relative to the anterior (A) compartment (Neufeld et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and confirmed by data in Figure 3F and G.

claim: The Ds gradient in the P compartment at WPP stage was indistinguishable from wildtype in en>RBF animals.
source: Nevertheless, the Ds gradient in the P compartment at WPP stage was indistinguishable from wildtype (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The Fat gradient flattened normally at the WPP stage in en>RBF animals.
source: The Fat gradient also flattened normally at the WPP stage (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The Ds gradient appears to directly scale to wing pouch volume as the pouch grows in size.
source: In summary, the Ds gradient appears to directly scale to wing pouch volume as the pouch grows in size.
evidence: This is an inference based on the trol(RNAi) and en>RBF experiments.

claim: Fat gradient flattening appears to be coupled to pouch volume rather than cell number or pouch area.
source: Fat gradient flattening also appears to be coupled to pouch volume rather than cell number or pouch area.
evidence: This is an inference based on the trol(RNAi) and en>RBF experiments.

claim: The dynamics of Fat and Ds atypical cadherins are coupled to a global physical feature of the wing.
source: Therefore, the dynamics of these atypical cadherins are coupled to a global physical feature of the wing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the volume-scaling observations.

claim: Loss-of-function fat mutants delay the larva-pupa transition and overgrow the wing disc.
source: Prior work had shown that loss-of-function fat mutants delay the larva-pupa transition and overgrow the wing disc (Bryant et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and confirmed by data in Figure 4.

claim: fat mutant larvae did not stop growing at 4.5 days AEL as wildtype larvae did, but continued to increase in weight for another day until they entered the non-feeding stage and pupated.
source: Mutant larvae did not stop growing at 4.5 days AEL as wildtype larvae did, but continued to increase in weight for another day until they entered the non-feeding stage and pupated (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by weight measurements shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The fat mutant larval notum and wing pouch grew at a faster rate than normal.
source: The mutant larval notum and wing pouch grew at a faster rate than normal, and at the larva-pupa transition, the wing pouch continued to grow (Figure 4C and D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by growth measurements shown in Figure 4C and D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: At the larva-pupa transition, the fat mutant wing pouch continued to grow.
source: The mutant larval notum and wing pouch grew at a faster rate than normal, and at the larva-pupa transition, the wing pouch continued to grow (Figure 4C and D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by growth measurements shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Loss-of-function ds mutants delayed the larva-pupa transition by 12 hr.
source: Loss-of-function ds mutants also delayed the larva-pupa transition but only by 12 hr.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ds mutant larvae continued to gain weight past the wildtype plateau, and they only ceased weight gain at the larva-pupa transition.
source: Mutant larvae continued to gain weight past the wildtype plateau, and they only ceased weight gain at the larva-pupa transition (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by weight measurements shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The ds mutant larval notum and wing pouch grew at a rate comparable to those of wildtype, but their growth period was extended.
source: The mutant larval notum and wing pouch grew at a rate comparable to those of wildtype, but their growth period was extended (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by growth measurements shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ds mutant notum ceased to grow prior to the larva-pupa transition, but the wing pouch only stopped growing at the WPP + 1 stage.
source: While the mutant notum ceased to grow prior to the larva-pupa transition, the wing pouch only stopped growing at the WPP + 1 stage (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by growth measurements shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Allometric growth of the fat and ds mutant wing pouch was significantly different from wildtype.
source: Allometric growth of the fat and ds mutant wing pouch was significantly different from wildtype (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by allometric growth data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Allometric growth of the ds and fat mutant wing pouches had a first phase that was more extended than normal and a second phase that was less extended than normal.
source: Allometric growth of the ds and fat mutant wing pouches had a first phase that was more extended than normal and a second phase that was less extended than normal (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by allometric growth data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Similar allometric growth trends were observed for the notum in fat and ds mutants.
source: Similar trends were observed for allometric growth of the notum in these mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by allometric growth data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RNAi against the ds gene resulted in near-complete depletion of Ds protein in the wing pouch.
source: RNAi against the ds gene resulted in near-complete depletion of Ds protein in the wing pouch (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Knockdown of Ds in the wing pouch had no effect on body growth of larvae, and animals reached a normal final weight setpoint.
source: As expected, knockdown of Ds in the wing pouch had no effect on body growth of larvae, and animals reached a normal final weight setpoint (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by weight measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: ds is not required in the wing to limit body growth.
source: Thus, ds is not required in the wing to limit body growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that wing-specific ds knockdown does not affect body growth.

claim: Notum growth in nub>ds(RNAi) animals was similar to controls.
source: Notum growth in nub >ds(RNAi) animals was similar to controls, which would be expected if the gene was not required in the wing pouch for notum growth control (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by notum growth measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–F.

claim: The nub>ds(RNAi) wing pouch grew at a faster rate than normal.
source: However, the nub >ds(RNAi) wing pouch grew at a faster rate than normal.
evidence: This is supported by growth measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The nub>ds(RNAi) wing pouch was 28% larger at the WPP stage and continued to grow until it was 42% larger at the WPP + 1 stage.
source: The wing pouch was 28% larger at the WPP stage and continued to grow until it was 42% larger at the WPP + 1 stage (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by volume measurements shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Knockdown of Ds in the wing pouch caused the entire allometric relationship to shift such that nub>ds(RNAi) wings were consistently bigger for their given body size.
source: Knockdown of Ds in the wing pouch caused the entire allometric relationship to shift such that nub >ds(RNAi) wings were consistently bigger for their given body size.
evidence: This is supported by allometric growth data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Ds is required in the wing pouch to tune down the allometric relationship of the wing to the body.
source: Thus, it appears that Ds is required in the wing pouch to tune down the allometric relationship of the wing to the body.
evidence: This is an inference based on the allometric growth shift observed in ds(RNAi) animals.

claim: nub-Gal4 driving UAS-GFP(RNAi) resulted in virtually complete elimination of Fat-GFP expression in the wing pouch.
source: There was virtually complete elimination of Fat-GFP expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Less than 5% of Fat-GFP remained after RNAi treatment.
source: Correcting for background fluorescence, we estimated that less than 5% of Fat-GFP remained after RNAi treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Knockdown of Fat-GFP had a weak effect during mid third instar.
source: Knockdown of Fat-GFP had a weak effect during mid third instar (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is supported by volume measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The nub>fat-GFP(RNAi) wing pouch was 15% larger than normal by the WPP stage, and 42% larger than normal by the WPP + 1 stage.
source: but the wing pouch was 15% larger than normal by the WPP stage, and 42% larger than normal by the WPP + 1 stage (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by volume measurements shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2G.

claim: The nub>fat-GFP(RNAi) wing pouch was of comparable size to the nub>ds(RNAi) wing pouch at WPP + 1 stage.
source: The nub >fat-GFP(RNAi) wing pouch was of comparable size to the nub >ds(RNAi) wing pouch at WPP + 1 stage (Figure 5—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is supported by volume measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2H.

claim: Adult wings from nub>fat-GFP(RNAi) individuals were 40% larger than controls.
source: Adult wings from nub >fat-GFP(RNAi) individuals were also 40% larger than controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: This is supported by adult wing area measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2I.

claim: Fat and Ds are autonomously required to inhibit wing pouch growth during the mid-to-late third instar and its transition to the pupal stage.
source: Thus, Fat and Ds are autonomously required to inhibit wing pouch growth during the mid-to-late third instar and its transition to the pupal stage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the wing-specific RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Knockdown of ds in the dorsal compartment caused the D/V ratio of compartment size to increase by 60%.
source: Knockdown of ds caused the D/V ratio of compartment size to increase by 60% (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by compartment size measurements shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Overall wing pouch size was unaffected by ap>ds(RNAi) knockdown.
source: Overall wing pouch size was unaffected by ap >ds(RNAi) knockdown (Figure 5H)
evidence: This is supported by wing pouch area measurements shown in Figure 5H.

claim: There are mechanisms in which the compartments sense overall pouch size, resulting in undergrowth of one compartment when there is overgrowth in the other compartment.
source: since there are mechanisms in which the compartments sense overall pouch size, resulting in undergrowth of one compartment when there is overgrowth in the other compartment (Diaz-Benjumea and Cohen, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and explains the observation in Figure 5H.

claim: en>ds(RNAi) increased the P/A ratio of compartment size by 63%.
source: After knockdown, the P/A ratio of compartment size was increased by 63% and 23% in en >ds(RNAi) and en >fat(RNAi) wing pouches, respectively (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is supported by compartment size measurements shown in Figure 5L.

claim: en>fat(RNAi) increased the P/A ratio of compartment size by 23%.
source: After knockdown, the P/A ratio of compartment size was increased by 63% and 23% in en >ds(RNAi) and en >fat(RNAi) wing pouches, respectively (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is supported by compartment size measurements shown in Figure 5L.

claim: en>fat ds(RNAi) showed an increase in the P/A ratio by 193%, an effect greater than the sum of effects from knockdown of each individual gene alone.
source: en >fat ds(RNAi) showed an increase in the P/A ratio by 193%, an effect greater than the sum of effects from knockdown of each individual gene alone (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is supported by compartment size measurements shown in Figure 5L.

claim: en>fat(RNAi), en>ds(RNAi), and en>fat ds(RNAi) affected overall wing pouch size with respective 10%, 19%, and 32% increases.
source: en >fat(RNAi), en >ds(RNAi), and en >fat ds(RNAi) affected overall wing pouch size to a lesser extent, with respective 10%, 19%, and 32% increases (Figure 5M).
evidence: This is supported by wing pouch area measurements shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Fat and Ds have autonomous effects on wing pouch growth consistent with fat and ds mutant phenotypes.
source: In conclusion, we found that Fat and Ds have autonomous effects on wing pouch growth consistent with fat and ds mutant phenotypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the compartment-specific RNAi experiments.

claim: The autonomous RNAi knockdown phenotypes were less severe than those of whole-body loss of fat and ds, suggesting there might be additional, non-autonomous requirements for Fat/Ds in wing growth.
source: However, the autonomous RNAi knockdown phenotypes were less severe than those of whole-body loss of fat and ds, suggesting there might be additional, non-autonomous requirements for Fat/Ds in wing growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of RNAi and mutant phenotypes.

claim: The number of ds(RNAi) cells in the D compartment was 42% higher than the wildtype control.
source: The number of ds(RNAi) cells in the D compartment was 42% higher than the wildtype control (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The average size of ds(RNAi) cells in the D compartment, as measured by apical domain area, was unchanged.
source: The average size of ds(RNAi) cells in the D compartment, as measured by apical domain area, was unchanged (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by cell size measurements shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The enhanced size of ds(RNAi) wing pouches is primarily driven by an increase in cell number.
source: Thus, the enhanced size of ds(RNAi) wing pouches is primarily driven by an increase in cell number.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell number and cell size measurements.

claim: There is little to no apoptosis in the third instar larval wing pouch.
source: There is little to no apoptosis reported to occur in the third instar larval wing pouch (Milán et al., 1997), which we confirmed by anti-caspase 3 staining (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and confirmed by the authors' own observations.

claim: The average time for third instar larval wing pouch cells to transit M phase is 20.5 min or 0.34 hr.
source: We found the average time for third instar larval wing pouch cells to transit M phase to be 20.5 min or 0.34 hr (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average M phase time of 20.5 min is highly similar to previous measurements.
source: which is highly similar to previous measurements (Wartlick et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a citation to previous work.

claim: The average cell cycle time linearly scales with wing pouch volume during the mid-to-late third instar.
source: Our results corroborated these reports but also expanded upon them, finding that the average cell cycle time linearly scales with wing pouch volume during the mid-to-late third instar (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle time measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The estimated scaling coefficient predicts that the cell cycle length increases 16 hr as wing pouch volume increases by 1 nL.
source: The estimated scaling coefficient (slope of the linear fit) predicts that the cell cycle length increases 16 hr as wing pouch volume increases by 1 nL.
evidence: This is based on the linear regression analysis of cell cycle time versus wing pouch volume data.

claim: The nub>ds(RNAi) cell cycle time linearly scaled with wing pouch volume.
source: The nub >ds(RNAi) cell cycle time linearly scaled with wing pouch volume (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle time measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The scaling coefficient for ds(RNAi) cells was much smaller than wildtype (p=6.2 × 10–4).
source: However, the scaling coefficient for ds(RNAi) cells was much smaller than wildtype (Figure 6—source data 1; p=6.2 × 10–4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of linear regression slopes.

claim: In ds(RNAi) cells, cell cycle duration was not lengthening as rapidly as normal and so cell cycle times were consistently shorter.
source: This meant that cell cycle duration was not lengthening as rapidly as normal and so cell cycle times were consistently shorter.
evidence: This is an inference based on the smaller scaling coefficient in ds(RNAi) cells.

claim: The scaling coefficient for nub>fat-GFP(RNAi) cells was much smaller than wildtype (p=3.1 × 10–4).
source: The scaling coefficient for nub >fat-GFP(RNAi) cells was also much smaller than wildtype (Figure 6—source data 1; p=3.1 × 10–4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of linear regression slopes.

claim: The model predictions of wing pouch growth were very close to the observed pouch growth for wildtype wings and for wings in which either Fat or Ds were knocked down by RNAi.
source: Strikingly, the model predictions were very close to the observed pouch growth for wildtype wings and for wings in which either Fat or Ds were knocked down by RNAi.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of model simulations with experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: During the mid-to-late third instar, cell cycle control primarily accounts for wing pouch growth.
source: This agreement between quantitative model predictions and experiment indicates that during the mid-to-late third instar, cell cycle control primarily accounts for wing pouch growth
evidence: This is an inference based on the agreement between model predictions and experimental observations.

claim: The effects of Fat/Ds on wing pouch growth are primarily exerted by their regulation of cell cycle dynamics.
source: and the effects of Fat/Ds on wing pouch growth are primarily exerted by their regulation of cell cycle dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the agreement between model predictions and experimental observations.

claim: During the third instar, Fat and Ds regulate a mechanism that couples the duration of the cell cycle to overall wing pouch size.
source: In summary, during the third instar, Fat and Ds regulate a mechanism that couples the duration of the cell cycle to overall wing pouch size.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the cell cycle scaling data.

claim: Fat and Ds are not essential for the coupling mechanism itself but rather they tune the mechanism so as to ensure the growth rate of the wing is attenuated relative to the body.
source: They are not essential for the coupling mechanism itself but rather they tune the mechanism so as to ensure the growth rate of the wing is attenuated relative to the body.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cell cycle still scales with wing size in RNAi knockdown, but with a different coefficient.

claim: Fat and Ds tuning of the cell cycle mechanism coordinates the relative scaling of the wing to the final body size.
source: This coordinates the relative scaling of the wing to the final body size.
evidence: This is an inference based on the allometric growth data and cell cycle regulation.

claim: nub>ds drastically altered the Ds protein gradient.
source: This drastically altered the Ds protein gradient (compare Figure 2C vs. Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The altered Ds gradient caused a change in the Fat gradient.
source: The altered Ds gradient caused a change in the Fat gradient (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In nub>ds animals, the Fat gradient peak became skewed to the anterior, and the gradient did not flatten at the WPP stage.
source: The gradient peak became skewed to the anterior, and the gradient did not flatten at the WPP stage.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The growth curve of the third instar wing pouch in nub>ds animals was indistinguishable from wildtype, and wing growth ceased normally at the WPP stage of the larva-pupa transition.
source: The growth curve of the third instar wing pouch was indistinguishable from wildtype, and wing growth ceased normally at the WPP stage of the larva-pupa transition (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by growth measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Drastically altering the Ds gradient does not impact wing growth.
source: This result suggests that drastically altering the Ds gradient does not impact wing growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nub>ds experiment results.

claim: ds>Ds overexpression strongly amplified Ds expression in the wing pouch while its gradient pattern was preserved.
source: Ds expression in the wing pouch was strongly amplified while its gradient pattern was preserved (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In ds>Ds wing pouches, the Fat protein gradient resembled wildtype.
source: In such ds >Ds wing pouches, the Fat protein gradient resembled wildtype (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: The ds>Ds wing pouch was approximately 12% larger than wildtype at the WPP stage, as well as in the adult.
source: Interestingly, the wing pouch was approximately 12% larger than wildtype at the WPP stage, as well as in the adult (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by volume and area measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: The scaling coefficient between cell cycle time and wing pouch volume for ds>Ds was slightly smaller than wildtype, but not significantly (p=0.108).
source: Although the scaling coefficient was slightly smaller than wildtype, it was not significant (Figure 7—source data 1; p=0.108).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of linear regression slopes shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Graded overexpression of Ds only weakly affects growth.
source: Thus, graded overexpression of Ds only weakly affects growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ds>Ds experiment results.

claim: Cells appear to be relatively insensitive to the levels and pattern of Ds expression in terms of their growth.
source: Overall, cells appear to be relatively insensitive to the levels and pattern of Ds expression in terms of their growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Ds manipulation experiments.

claim: In nub>fat HA animals, both transgenic and endogenous Fat gradients did not diminish in magnitude as larvae approached pupariation.
source: Strikingly, both transgenic and endogenous Fat gradients did not diminish in magnitude as larvae approached pupariation.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 7H and I.

claim: In nub>fat HA animals, the Fat gradients did not flatten at the WPP stage but only did so at the later WPP +1 stage.
source: Moreover, the gradients did not flatten at the WPP stage but only did so at the later WPP +1 stage.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 7H and I.

claim: The relationship between the cell cycle time in the nub>fat HA wing pouch and wing pouch size was indistinguishable from wildtype.
source: The relationship between the cell cycle time in the nub >fat HA wing pouch and wing pouch size was indistinguishable from wildtype (Figure 7J and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle time measurements shown in Figure 7J.

claim: Final wing pouch size in nub>fat HA animals was normal.
source: This was consistent with the observation that final wing pouch size in nub >fat HA animals was normal (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by volume measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Fat and Ds gradient dynamics do not appear to play a significant role in wing growth control.
source: In summary, Fat and Ds gradient dynamics do not appear to play a significant role in wing growth control.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Fat and Ds manipulation experiments.

claim: Fat and Ds attenuate the rate of third instar wing growth so that it properly scales with body growth via a complex allosteric relationship.
source: Fat and Ds attenuate the rate of third instar wing growth so that it properly scales with body growth via a complex allosteric relationship.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the allometric growth data and RNAi experiments.

claim: Fat and Ds tune the rate at which the cell cycle progressively lengthens in a linear fashion as the third instar wing grows in size by enhancing this rate of lengthening.
source: They do so by tuning the rate at which the cell cycle progressively lengthens in a linear fashion as the third instar wing grows in size. This rate of lengthening is enhanced by the actions of Fat and Ds.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the cell cycle scaling data.

claim: It has been long known that the cell cycle in the wing disc slows down, with a cell doubling time of 6 hr during the second instar increasing to 30 hr by the end of third instar.
source: It has been long known that the cell cycle in the wing disc slows down, with a cell doubling time of 6 hr during the second instar increasing to 30 hr by the end of third instar (Fain and Stevens, 1982; Bryant and Levinson, 1985; Bittig et al., 2009; Martín et al., 2009; Wartlick et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A link has been found between doubling time of wing disc cells and the morphogen Dpp.
source: A link has been found between doubling time of wing disc cells and the morphogen Dpp (Wartlick et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Dpp is continually synthesized in a stripe of cells at the AP midline of the wing disc and is transported to form a stably graded distribution of protein that is bilaterally symmetric around the midline.
source: Dpp is continually synthesized in a stripe of cells at the AP midline of the wing disc and is transported to form a stably graded distribution of protein that is bilaterally symmetric around the midline (Teleman and Cohen, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Dpp gradient precisely scales to remain proportional to the size of the growing disc by a mechanism involving the extracellular protein Pentagone and tissue-scale transport of recycled Dpp after endocytosis.
source: The gradient precisely scales to remain proportional to the size of the growing disc by a mechanism involving the extracellular protein Pentagone and tissue-scale transport of recycled Dpp after endocytosis (Ben-Zvi et al., 2011; Hamaratoglu et al., 2011; Wartlick et al., 2011; Wartlick et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2020; Romanova-Michaelides et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: As the Dpp gradient scales with the wing, the local concentration of Dpp each wing cell experiences continuously increases over time.
source: As the gradient scales with the wing, the local concentration of Dpp each wing cell experiences continuously increases over time (Wartlick et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The doubling time of wing disc cells was found to strongly correlate with the temporal increase in Dpp concentration, such that an average cell divides when Dpp increases by 40% relative to its level at the beginning of the division cycle.
source: The doubling time of wing disc cells was found to strongly correlate with this temporal increase in Dpp concentration, such that an average cell divides when Dpp increases by 40% relative to its level at the beginning of the division cycle (Wartlick et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The progressive lengthening of the cell cycle may be caused by a slowing rate of increase in local Dpp concentration over time.
source: The correlation was observed throughout larval development, indicating that the progressive lengthening of the cell cycle may be caused by a slowing rate of increase in local Dpp concentration over time.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the cited correlation.

claim: Fat inhibits apico-cortical localization of the atypical myosin Dachs, consistent with genetically antagonistic roles played by fat and dachs.
source: Fat inhibits apico-cortical localization of the atypical myosin Dachs, consistent with genetically antagonistic roles played by fat and dachs (Cho and Irvine, 2004; Mao et al., 2006; Mao et al., 2006; Brittle et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Loss of dachs suppresses overproliferation of wing disc cells when a constitutively-active form of the Dpp receptor protein is expressed.
source: Loss of dachs also suppresses overproliferation of wing disc cells when a constitutively-active form of the Dpp receptor protein is expressed (Rogulja et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of fat enhances Dpp signaling within wing disc cells.
source: In contrast, loss of fat enhances Dpp signaling within wing disc cells (Tyler and Baker, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: It is possible that local Ds-Fat signaling between third instar wing cells attenuates their sensitivity to Dpp as a mitogen.
source: Therefore, it is possible that local Ds-Fat signaling between third instar wing cells attenuates their sensitivity to Dpp as a mitogen.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the cited literature.

claim: If Ds-Fat signaling attenuates Dpp sensitivity, it would require a larger temporal increase in Dpp concentration to trigger cells to divide.
source: It would then require a larger temporal increase in Dpp concentration to trigger cells to divide.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the speculative hypothesis.

claim: The model that Ds-Fat signaling attenuates Dpp sensitivity is consistent with the observation that third instar wing cells do not lengthen their cell cycle as rapidly as normal when Fat or Ds are knocked down.
source: This model is consistent with our observation that third instar wing cells do not lengthen their cell cycle as rapidly as normal when Fat or Ds are knocked down.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the speculative model with experimental observations.

claim: Dpp signaling represses Brinker, and it has been proposed that Brinker is the primary mediator of growth control by Dpp.
source: Dpp signaling represses Brinker, and it has been proposed that Brinker is the primary mediator of growth control by Dpp (Schwank et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Fat and Dpp may act in parallel rather than sequentially to regulate growth.
source: Moreover, Fat and Dpp may act in parallel rather than sequentially to regulate growth (Schwank et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous work cited in the text.

claim: Ds-Fat signaling via the Hippo pathway may regulate the cell cycle duration of wing pouch cells independent of Dpp.
source: Therefore, Ds-Fat signaling via the Hippo pathway may regulate the cell cycle duration of wing pouch cells independent of Dpp.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the cited literature.

claim: Fat/Ds regulates growth of the wing pouch by a feedforward recruitment of neighboring hinge/notum cells to become wing pouch cells.
source: Another known mechanism by which Fat/Ds regulates growth of the wing pouch is by a feedforward recruitment of neighboring hinge/notum cells to become wing pouch cells (Zecca and Struhl, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The feedforward recruitment mechanism does not involve cell proliferation control.
source: This mechanism does not involve cell proliferation control.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of the feedforward mechanism.

claim: Analysis of Fat/Ds function during the mid-to-late third instar suggests that they are not working through the feedforward mechanism to any large extent.
source: Our analysis of Fat/Ds function during the mid-to-late third instar suggests that they are not working through the feedforward mechanism to any large extent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: Model simulations of wing pouch growth assuming Fat/Ds only control cell cycle duration strongly fit with measurements of pouch growth during the third instar.
source: Model simulations of wing pouch growth assuming Fat/Ds only control cell cycle duration strongly fit with our measurements of pouch growth during the third instar (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Any contribution of Fat/Ds towards recruitment of pouch cells must be minor at the mid-to-late third instar stage.
source: This would argue that any contribution of Fat/Ds towards recruitment of pouch cells must be minor at this stage of larval growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: The Ds expression pattern has a graded distribution with a steep slope in the proximal region of the wing pouch (near the pouch border) and a shallow slope in the distal region of the pouch (near the pouch center).
source: The Ds expression pattern has a graded distribution with a steep slope in the proximal region of the wing pouch (near the pouch border) and a shallow slope in the distal region of the pouch (near the pouch center).
evidence: This is a summary of the Ds gradient observations.

claim: Fat protein is distributed in a gradient that is complementary to the Ds protein gradient – Fat is most abundant in cells where Ds levels are minimal and its gradient is most shallow.
source: We find that Fat protein is distributed in a gradient that is complementary to the Ds protein gradient – Fat is most abundant in cells where Ds levels are minimal and its gradient is most shallow.
evidence: This is a summary of the Fat gradient observations.

claim: Global loss of Ds affects Fat distribution across the wing pouch such that Fat is abnormally elevated near the pouch border while remaining unchanged at the pouch center, effectively making a more shallow Fat gradient.
source: Global loss of Ds affects Fat distribution across the wing pouch such that Fat is abnormally elevated near the pouch border while remaining unchanged at the pouch center, effectively making a more shallow Fat gradient.
evidence: This is a summary of the ds mutant Fat gradient observations.

claim: Cells might repress Fat expression if they sense a steep Ds gradient.
source: This might suggest that cells repress Fat expression if they sense a steep Ds gradient.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the ds mutant results.

claim: Cells might repress Fat expression in a manner dependent on Ds levels.
source: Alternatively, cells might repress Fat expression in a manner dependent on Ds levels.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative interpretation of the ds mutant results.

claim: ds mutant clones exhibit upregulated Fat localized to junctions between mutant cells.
source: Indeed, ds mutant clones exhibit upregulated Fat localized to junctions between mutant cells (Ma et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Ectopically increasing Ds expression in central regions of the pouch with nub>ds did not repress Fat abundance in those regions.
source: However, these interpretations of loss-of-function experiments are complicated by our results manipulating the Ds gradient. Ectopically increasing Ds expression in central regions of the pouch with nub >ds did not repress Fat abundance in those regions.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from the nub>ds experiment.

claim: Amplifying the slope of the Ds gradient and boosting the maximal levels of Ds with ds>Ds did not lead to stronger repression of Fat near the pouch border.
source: Nor did amplifying the slope of the Ds gradient and boosting the maximal levels of Ds with ds >Ds lead to stronger repression of Fat near the pouch border.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from the ds>Ds experiment.

claim: The distribution of Fat is insensitive to the absolute level or differential in Ds abundance above some minimal level that is non-zero.
source: Thus, the distribution of Fat is insensitive to the absolute level or differential in Ds abundance above some minimal level that is non-zero.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Ds manipulation experiments.

claim: Below a minimal non-zero level of Ds, Fat is upregulated.
source: Below this minimum and Fat is somehow upregulated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ds mutant observations.

claim: It is tempting to speculate that heterophilic binding of Ds to Fat, either in trans or in cis, is responsible for Fat distribution regulation.
source: It is tempting to speculate that heterophilic binding of Ds to Fat, either in trans or in cis, is responsible (Hale et al., 2015; Fulford et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on cited literature.

claim: If heterophilic binding of Ds to Fat is responsible for Fat distribution regulation, then it is likely distinct from the stabilizing interactions that Ds has on Fat at cell junctions.
source: If so, then it is likely distinct from the stabilizing interactions that Ds has on Fat at cell junctions (Ma et al., 2003; Hale et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on cited literature and current observations.

claim: The graded distributions of Fat and Ds proteins across the pouch are not stable over time but become progressively more shallow as the larva-pupa transition is reached.
source: The graded distributions of Fat and Ds proteins across the pouch are not stable over time but become progressively more shallow as the larva-pupa transition is reached.
evidence: This is a summary of the gradient dynamics observations.

claim: For Ds, its gradient scales with the size of the wing pouch because the maximum and minimum limits of Ds-GFP abundance are conserved as the wing pouch grows.
source: For Ds, its gradient scales with the size of the wing pouch. This occurs because the maximum and minimum limits of Ds-GFP abundance are conserved as the wing pouch grows.
evidence: This is an inference based on the normalized gradient data.

claim: Dividing cells take up intermediate scalar values from their neighbors during growth, and over time the steepness of the Ds gradient consequently diminishes.
source: It would imply that dividing cells take up intermediate scalar values from their neighbors during growth, and over time the steepness of the Ds gradient consequently diminishes.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism to explain the gradient scaling.

claim: The mechanism of cells adopting intermediate levels of Ds from their neighbors by local sensing would explain why the Ds gradient scales with pouch volume and not cell number.
source: Such a mechanism would also explain why the Ds gradient scales with pouch volume and not cell number. Whether cells are many or few in number, if they adopt intermediate levels of Ds from their neighbors by local sensing, then the gradient scales as the tissue expands.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the volume-scaling observation.

claim: The observation of shallowing gradients of Fat and Ds expression fits with a long-standing model for growth regulation by Fat and Ds.
source: Our observation of shallowing gradients of Fat and Ds expression fits with a long-standing model for growth regulation by Fat and Ds.
evidence: This is a statement connecting current observations with previous models.

claim: Based on experiments with clones expressing Ds at different levels than their neighbors, it was suggested that Fat signaling is regulated by the steepness of a Ds gradient across a field of cells.
source: Based on experiments with clones expressing Ds at different levels than their neighbors, it was suggested that Fat signaling is regulated by the steepness of a Ds gradient across a field of cells (Rogulja et al., 2008; Willecke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a model from previous work cited in the text.

claim: According to the gradient model, a steep gradient of Ds inactivates Fat signaling (stimulates growth), whereas a shallow gradient activates Fat signaling (inhibits growth).
source: A steep gradient of Ds inactivates Fat signaling (stimulates growth), whereas a shallow gradient activates Fat signaling (inhibits growth).
evidence: This is a description of the gradient model from previous work.

claim: According to the gradient model, a progressively shallowing gradient of Ds would progressively slow down growth, which is what occurs during the third instar.
source: Thus, a progressively shallowing gradient of Ds would progressively slow down growth, which is what occurs during the third instar.
evidence: This is a prediction of the gradient model that appears consistent with observations.

claim: A shallowing gradient of Fat might also fit within the gradient model of growth control.
source: Although the model did not consider a Fat gradient, our finding a shallowing gradient of Fat might also fit within this gradient model of growth control.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the gradient model.

claim: When Fat or Ds protein graded distributions in the wing pouch were manipulated, there was little or no effect on wing growth.
source: However, when we manipulated the graded distributions of Fat or Ds protein in the wing pouch, there was little or no effect on its growth.
evidence: This is a summary of the gradient manipulation experiments.

claim: Enhancing the gradient of Fat by its overexpression did not stimulate growth.
source: Enhancing the gradient of Fat by its overexpression did not stimulate growth.
evidence: This is based on the nub>fat HA experiment results.

claim: Amplifying the Ds gradient by severalfold overexpression using ds>Ds led to only a weak growth response.
source: Nor did amplifying the Ds gradient by severalfold overexpression using ds >Ds lead to greatly enhanced growth but only a weak response.
evidence: This is based on the ds>Ds experiment results.

claim: The gradient manipulation results are not consistent with the gradient model.
source: These results are not consistent with the gradient model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gradient manipulation experiments.

claim: Loss of Fat and Ds diminishes the scaling coefficient that couples cell cycle time to pouch size, and this effect is constant over 36 hr of third instar growth.
source: Moreover, loss of Fat and Ds diminishes the scaling coefficient that couples cell cycle time to pouch size, and this effect is constant over 36 hr of third instar growth (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle time data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Ds and Fat are not progressively tuning their impact on growth rate of the wing, as the gradient model predicts.
source: Thus, Ds and Fat are not progressively tuning their impact on growth rate of the wing, as the gradient model predicts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the constant scaling coefficient effect over time.

claim: Third instar wing cells are tolerant of differences in Fat/Ds abundance.
source: Instead, we suggest that third instar wing cells are tolerant of differences in Fat/Ds abundance
evidence: This is an inference based on the gradient manipulation experiments.

claim: The Fat and Ds gradients may be linked to the planar cell polarity functions of these proteins.
